title: The Maharaja close
hook: forty years of a Punjab kingdom, from Lahore's open gate to the samadhi

segments.voice: Yesterday, sach, and your line, pride and honesty. Today, the story of the Maharaja comes to its close.

Lay two pictures side by side. In the first, a young chief with one eye rides through a gate of Lahore that someone inside has opened for him. In the second, a pale building with a gilded dome stands by the same city's Fort, holding his ashes. Everything in this part of the path happened between those two pictures. Histories count about forty years from the day he took Lahore to the day he died.
screen: `A GATE OPENED IN LAHORE.` → `A SAMADHI BY THE FORT.` → `EVERYTHING IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: A boy born in Gujranwala, scarred by smallpox and blind in one eye, led his misl young, with help around him. Lahore opened its gate to him. He took the title of Maharaja, but ruled as the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government in the Khalsa's name. Look at what he built: gold on the Harmandir, a river line on the Sutlej he chose to keep, an army drilled in new ways by officers from many lands, Hari Singh Nalwa on the frontier, Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar joining the kingdom, the Koh-i-Noor on his arm, a court of many faiths, painters at work, gifts to Patna and Nanded, and a reputation for rarely ordering death. And Maharani Jind Kaur, the youngest queen, whose hardest days are still ahead. Then what he couldn't hold. He bowed at the Akal Takht and accepted its rebuke, so even he answered to something above the throne. But he left no settled way to hand on what he'd built. After he died, the kingdom came apart in the hands of rivals: two heirs lost, Sher Singh killed, a child on the throne, the army louder than the court. A kingdom so much one man's work was fragile without him. Forty years is a single working life: long enough to change the map, short enough that people who saw it begin could see it end. That's the sorrow in this story, and the honesty too. Some things are great and brief at once. Tomorrow a new part of the path begins, and it's harder: war with the British.
screen: `THE RISE: FROM A MISL TO LAHORE.` · `WHAT HE BUILT.` · `WHAT HE COULDN'T HOLD.` · `GREAT AND BRIEF AT ONCE.` · then, large: `FORTY YEARS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something good in your life that didn't last as long as you wanted: a friendship, a home, a season, a person. Picture its beginning, then what it built in you, then the end, without rushing past it, and notice what's still with you from it, even now. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.
Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government in the Khalsa's name, the title Ranjit Singh ruled under through the forty years from Lahore's open gate to his samadhi.
Your line: forty years. One working life, and a map that changed. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign as the time of a Sikh kingdom in the Punjab, and tell its story from his taking of Lahore to his death, and the troubles that followed.

chat.says: Why did Ranjit Singh's kingdom fall apart so fast after he died?
options: So much of it was his own work, and he left no settled way to hand it on.
The British conquered it in battle the very same year he died.
His heirs freely gave it away to the Afghans to keep the peace.
chat.meaning: He left no settled way to hand on what he'd built; after his death rivals pulled it apart: heirs lost, Sher Singh killed, a child enthroned.
